newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis "stable" despite rebel brinksmanship.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis "stable" despite rebel brinksmanship.

text.p: Gunshots in the night and media grandstanding by Marxist rebel hostage-takers have provided almost daily drama in their war of nerves with Peru's government.
But officials and analysts say the 27-day stand-off has become more stable and manageable with the passage of time.

The rebels are honing a form of brinksmanship by raising and deflating hopes of negotiations with the government of President Alberto Fujimori, but by doing so they are also helping define the rules and limits of the stand-off, some analysts say.

Government officials from Fujimori on down say they are settling in for what may prove a very long haul, drawing parallels with hostage situations in other countries which have dragged on for months and saying a certain stability and routine has been achieved.

The rebels, as leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini quipped to the government's chief negotiator last week, "are not going anywhere" and appear to relish the prospect of drawing out their time in the spotlight for as long as possible.
"They are desperate for publicity," a senior government source told Reuters recently.

"The rules get clearer each time the police do not shoot back," said one political analyst, who declined to be named, explaining that the rebels seemed to be testing the limits of the government's tolerance.
The government source added though that the Fujimori administration, too, saw time as its ally.
"Time is working in our favour," the source said. "There is a point of equilibrium now. This may take some time."

Each time the rebels flirt with expectations that the siege could still end bloodily -- as they did again on Friday by firing bursts from their rifles when a helicopter flew too close overhead -- they attract the attention they crave for their cause from Peruvian and world media camped out at the site.

Playing on hopes of a negotiated end to the stand-off -- as they also did at the weekend by agreeing to meet government negotiator Domingo Palermo, allowing expectations to build and then administering a well-timed dose of cold water -- has had the same effect.

Each successful publicity stunt or negotiating coup de theatre drags out the crisis but also makes it harder to make good on their initial threats to shoot the hostages if their main demands, for the liberation of some 400 jailed colleagues, are not met.

"The failure of the face-to-face meeting between Palermo and Cerpa effectively prolongs the stand-off," said Washington-based Sandy Markwick of consulting firm Control Risks Group, which monitors political risk to businesses around the world.
The government has developed an agile negotiating machinery through which it was able to provide an immediate riposte to the rebel stance.
"The government's rapid counterproposal...means that the initiative to move the crisis forward was quickly returned to the rebel camp," Markwick told Reuters.
He added though: "The rebels retain considerable leverage because of the number and prominence of the remaining hostages."

The 74 hostages left include top Peruvian government and security officials, Japanese diplomats and businessmen and President Alberto Fujimori's brother Pedro as well as the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors to Peru.
The government's counterproposal was to invite the rebels to join the Vatican, the Red Cross and the government in a joint commission to end the crisis.
The rebel response: a request for a Peruvian TV crew to broadcast their reply.

Fujimori told reporters last week that the desire of the rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) to improve their image and sell themselves as Robin Hood-type defenders of the poor -- an image he rejects -- effectively tied their hands as regards threats to the hostages.

"It is not a mistake to think that after the MRTA's TV and media campaign, it can't hurt anyone, because all that it has gained might be lost," Fujimori told Newsweek magazine. "With this stability it is possible to talk."
